title: Storage engines and indexes
summary: A database's behaviour under load is decided by how it arranges data on disk and how it finds rows again. This lesson gives the amplification vocabulary, contrasts B-tree engines that update pages in place with LSM engines that append and merge, puts the two row layouts, the column layout and the object store into one decision table, explains index types and their write cost, shows what multiversion concurrency costs in dead rows, and reads a query plan, with a worked comparison of the two engine families for an event log.

blocks.text: Google's Bigtable, the design most LSM engines descend from, stores a tablet as a commit log plus an in-memory memtable and a sequence of immutable SSTables on GFS. A read merges the memtable and all SSTables; minor compactions flush the memtable, merging compactions bound the number of files, and a major compaction periodically rewrites a tablet into one SSTable with no deletion markers. Clients can ask for a Bloom filter per SSTable in a locality group, which the paper reports drastically reduces disk seeks for reads of rows that do not exist.

The RocksDB team's tuning guide tells operators to find the bottleneck resource first and then move the amplification trade-off with compaction. Write amplification is measured as the disk write bandwidth from iostat divided by the database write rate; leveled compaction is the default and is chosen when space and reads matter, universal when ingest must be cheap; compaction is triggered when level 0 reaches four files; and Bloom filters default to about 10 bits per key.

blocks.caption: Bits per key against the share of misses a Bloom filter catches, from the RocksDB wiki.
columns: effectiveness relative to 100 bits per key

blocks.text: Amazon S3 is built on millions of hard disks, and its engineering, as Werner Vogels describes it, is about heat as much as capacity. Objects are erasure coded rather than fully replicated so that durability does not cost a full copy per replica; each object is encoded across tens of drives, and different objects are deliberately placed on different sets of drives so that one customer's accesses spread over a very large number of disks. The post notes that a burst from thousands of parallel functions can be served by over a million individual disks, and that individual workloads are bursty while the aggregate is smooth.

PostgreSQL's own documentation prescribes the operational routine for a B-tree engine under MVCC: vacuum every table regularly to reclaim dead row versions, refresh planner statistics and the visibility map, and freeze old transaction ids before wraparound; build indexes concurrently on live tables; and read EXPLAIN ANALYZE with BUFFERS before and after any index change.

A storage engine has two jobs: make a write durable and find a row again. Everything else about a database's behaviour under load follows from how it does those two things on a disk, where sequential writes are cheap, random writes are expensive and a page is the unit of transfer. The engine chooses how data is arranged, when it rewrites it in the background and what it reads to answer a lookup. This lesson gives the vocabulary for that trade-off, the two dominant engine families, the indexes built on them and the tools that show what an engine does with a query.

The RocksDB tuning guide gives the vocabulary as three amplification factors, each a ratio between what the application asked for and what the hardware did. Write amplification is bytes written to storage divided by bytes written to the database. Read amplification is the number of disk reads needed to answer one query. Space amplification is the size of the database files divided by the size of the data. Compaction, the background rewriting an engine does, is the knob that trades one against another.

blocks.caption: The three amplification factors, with the tuning guide's own examples.
rows: bytes written to disk per byte written to the database
writing 10 MB/s to the database and seeing 30 MB/s on disk is a write amplification of 3
sustained write rate: at a factor of 50 on a 500 MB/s disk the database can take 10 MB/s
a query that needs 5 pages has read amplification 5
latency and IOPS per query; cache hits are logical reads and still cost CPU
bytes on disk per byte of data
10 MB of data taking 100 MB on disk is a space amplification of 10
how much data fits on a host; set a hard limit so the disk does not fill

blocks.text: No engine wins all three. A B-tree reads a row in a handful of page visits but rewrites a page for every row it changes; a log-structured engine writes each row sequentially and again at every compaction, and consults several files to find it; old versions and sparse pages cost space in either. The LSM paper states the motivating case: for a table that only receives inserts, such as a transaction history, maintaining a B-tree index in real time effectively doubles the I/O cost of each transaction, so its design defers and batches the index changes instead.

Name the workload before the engine. Write down the ratio of writes to reads, whether reads are point lookups, short ranges or scans, how large the working set is next to memory, and how fast the data grows. Each engine family answers a different mix; none answers all of them.

subtopics.title: B-trees: sorted pages updated in place

blocks.text: A B-tree keeps rows, or index entries, in fixed-size pages sorted by key, with a tree of branch pages above them that points the search to the right leaf. The tree is balanced, so every leaf is the same number of levels below the root, and its depth grows logarithmically with the data: an index over millions of rows is typically four or five levels deep, and six is rare. A lookup therefore touches a known small number of pages, and the leaves are chained in order so that a range scan walks sideways once it has found its start.

Writes go to the page where the key belongs. The engine reads the page, changes it and writes it back, splitting it when it is full. Random keys mean random pages, so a stream of inserts with unordered keys dirties pages all over the file, and each dirtied page is eventually rewritten whole even if one row changed. To make this safe the engine first appends a record of the change to a write-ahead log, which is sequential and cheap; the data pages can then be written later and in batches, and a crash is repaired by replaying the log.

blocks.caption: What a B-tree engine does well and where it pays.
rows: a few page reads, predictable; the top levels stay in cache
efficient; leaves are linked in key order
a page read and a page write per change, scattered across the file; the log absorbs the burst, the pages still have to be written
pages run partly empty after splits and deletes, so the file is larger than the data
InnoDB, PostgreSQL's heap plus B-tree indexes, SQLite, most embedded key-value stores built for reads

blocks.text: The B-tree is the default for a reason: reads dominate most transactional workloads, and a design that gives every lookup a short, predictable path with sorted ranges for free is hard to beat. Its weakness shows when writes dominate and keys are random, which is exactly the history-table case the LSM paper opens with, or when the working set outgrows memory and each random write becomes a real disk operation.

Sequential keys turn B-tree writes into appends. A time-ordered or monotonically increasing primary key keeps inserts on the rightmost leaf, so the hot page stays in cache; a random UUID key spreads them over the whole tree.

subtopics.title: LSM trees: append, flush and merge

blocks.text: A log-structured merge engine never updates a page in place. A write goes to an append-only log for durability and into a sorted in-memory table, the memtable. When the memtable fills it is frozen and written out as an immutable sorted file; Bigtable called these SSTables and the flush a minor compaction. A read checks the memtable and then the sorted files, newest first, and merges what it finds. Left alone, the files pile up and every read has to consult more of them, so a background merging compaction reads several files and writes one, and a major compaction rewrites everything into a single file with no deletion markers left.

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  W[Write] --> L[Write-ahead log]
  W --> M[Memtable in memory]
  M -->|flush when full| S0[Level 0 sorted files]
  S0 -->|compaction| S1[Level 1 sorted files]
  S1 -->|compaction| S2[Deeper levels]
  R[Read] --> M
  R --> B[Bloom filters and block cache]
  B --> S0
  B --> S1
  B --> S2
blocks.legend: Writes append to the log and the memtable; flushes create level 0 files; compaction merges them downwards. Reads consult the memtable, then the Bloom filters and block cache, then the files.

blocks.text: Compaction is where the trade-off lives, and the RocksDB wiki names the two classic strategies. Leveled compaction, from the LSM paper, keeps each level as one sorted run about ten times larger than the one above and merges a level into the next when it overflows; it minimises space amplification at the cost of read and write amplification, because in the worst case every level rewrites each byte once more. Tiered compaction, called universal in RocksDB, keeps several sorted runs per level and merges runs of similar size; it minimises write amplification at the cost of read and space amplification.

blocks.caption: Leveled against tiered compaction, as the RocksDB wiki describes them.
rows: one; a level is one run, range-partitioned into files
higher: up to the fanout per level, less in practice
lower: a byte is rewritten once per size doubling
lower: one run per level to check
higher: every run in every level may hold the key
lowest; old versions are merged away quickly
higher, and briefly about double during a merge of the largest run
ingest-heavy stores that can spend disk and cache

blocks.text: Two structures keep reads tolerable. Each sorted file carries an index of its blocks, so a lookup inside a file costs about one disk seek, and a Bloom filter per file answers whether the file might contain the key, so most files are skipped without a read. The filter is a memory-for-I/O trade with sharply diminishing returns: the RocksDB wiki's table runs from a half of all misses caught at 1.5 bits per key to a false-positive rate of one percent at about 10 bits and a tenth of a percent at 15.5 bits, and 10 bits per key is its default.

Compaction debt is a failure mode. If writes arrive faster than compaction can merge, level 0 fills, reads slow down because they consult more files, and the engine finally stalls writes to catch up. Watch the pending compaction bytes and the level 0 file count as first-class health signals.

subtopics.title: Choosing the engine for an access pattern

blocks.text: The engine is chosen with the database, so the question in a design review is which family the data store you are about to pick belongs to, and whether its position on the amplification triangle matches the workload. The decision below covers the four layouts a designer meets: the two row-oriented engine families, the column layout used by analytical stores, and the object store that holds large immutable blobs. The lesson on choosing a data store takes the next step, from engine family to product.

blocks.caption: Which layout for which workload. Products are examples of the mechanism, not recommendations.

rows.option: B-tree engine (row store, update in place)
rows.pick_when: reads dominate, lookups are by key or short range, rows are updated in place, and transactions span several rows
rows.avoid_when: the workload is a firehose of inserts with random keys, or the dataset is far larger than memory and mostly written

rows.option: LSM engine (row store, append and merge)
rows.pick_when: writes dominate, keys arrive in any order, and reads are point lookups or recent ranges that Bloom filters and caches serve
rows.avoid_when: reads are scattered across old data and latency must be flat, or disk write bandwidth is already the bottleneck for compaction
rows.example: RocksDB, Apache Cassandra, Bigtable and its descendants

rows.pick_when: queries scan a few columns of many rows, aggregate, and tolerate batch ingestion; compression of same-typed values matters
rows.avoid_when: the access is single-row reads and writes, or rows must be updated in place at high rate
rows.example: ClickHouse, data warehouses, Parquet files on object storage

rows.pick_when: objects are large, written once and read whole or by range, and durability per byte must be cheap
rows.avoid_when: the application needs small random updates, listing by secondary attributes, or transactions across objects
rows.example: Amazon S3 and other object stores, with metadata in a database beside them

blocks.text: Pick the engine family from the dominant access path and let the second path pay. A read-heavy table with occasional writes belongs on a B-tree; an ingest firehose belongs on an LSM; a scan-and-aggregate workload belongs on columns; blobs belong in an object store with their metadata elsewhere. When one table has two dominant paths, that is the signal for two stores, and the next lesson prices it.

A column layout stores each column's values together instead of each row's, so a query that touches three columns of a billion-row table reads three streams and skips the rest, and values of one type compress well because they sit side by side. The price is that reading or changing one whole row touches every column file, which is why these stores ingest in batches and serve analytics, not transactions. Many of them are log-structured underneath: inserts create immutable parts that a background merge combines, the same append-and-merge shape as an LSM tree applied to column files.

blocks.caption: Row and column layouts for the same table.
rows: sum of one column over all rows
reads every page of the table
a write to every column file, so inserts are batched into parts
strong; same-typed values side by side

blocks.text: An object store is the database when the data is blobs: images, logs, backups, model weights, data-lake files. Its contract is a key, an immutable object, a range read and very high durability per byte at low cost; it offers no secondary indexes, no in-place updates and no transactions across objects, so the design pairs it with a small metadata store that holds the keys and attributes. The S3 post below describes the mechanism that makes this cheap at scale: erasure coding instead of full replication, and spreading each customer's objects over a very large number of disks so that bursts are served in parallel.

Analytical and blob workloads leave the transactional engine. Copy events into a column store for reporting and put files in an object store with their metadata in the relational database; the lesson on choosing a data store prices what the second store costs.

An index is a second structure that finds rows by something other than their position, and in PostgreSQL every index is secondary: the table is a heap, and each index maps key values to row locations. The default is a B-tree, which serves equality, range and ordered retrieval. The other types exist because some questions are not about ordering: GIN is an inverted index for values that contain many elements, such as arrays, JSON documents and full-text tokens, and BRIN stores a summary per range of physical blocks and stays tiny on very large tables whose physical order follows the indexed column.

blocks.caption: PostgreSQL's index types and the question each answers.
rows: one entry per row; a page write per insert
long opaque keys compared for equality
one entry per element; slower to update
range on a physically ordered column
a summary per block range; very small

blocks.text: Shape matters as much as type. In a multicolumn B-tree the leading columns decide how much of the index a query can skip: equality conditions on the leading columns, plus a range on the first column without one, narrow the scan, while a condition only on a trailing column scans the whole index. A partial index covers only the rows that match a predicate, which keeps a hot subset small and avoids indexing values too common for the planner to use. An index that holds every column a query needs allows an index-only scan that skips the table, when the visibility map says the page's rows are visible to everyone.

Every index is paid for on every write. An insert adds an entry to each index, an update that changes an indexed column removes one and adds another, and each is a page read and a page write somewhere in a tree. A table with eight indexes does nine writes per insert and holds nine structures in cache. The discipline is to add an index for a measured query, name the query in the migration, and remove indexes that no plan uses.

Building an index on a live table is itself a decision. A standard build locks out writes until it finishes, which on a large table is an outage; a concurrent build blocks no inserts, updates or deletes, at the cost of two scans of the table and a longer run, and if it fails it leaves an invalid index to drop and retry.
One index per measured query shape, built concurrently, justified by the plan before and after. An index nobody can name the query for is write cost with no reader.

Multiversion concurrency control is how a relational engine lets readers and writers work at once. Each statement sees a snapshot of the data as of some moment, regardless of what other transactions are doing, and the locks taken for reading do not conflict with the locks taken for writing, so in PostgreSQL's words reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading. The engine achieves this by keeping versions: an update creates a new row version and leaves the old one in place for any transaction whose snapshot can still see it.

The versions are the cost. An update or delete does not remove the old row; it becomes a dead version once no transaction can see it, and the space it occupies is reclaimed only when VACUUM runs over the table and its indexes. If vacuum falls behind the write rate, tables and indexes bloat, scans read dead rows, and the visibility map that index-only scans depend on goes stale. Vacuum also has a second duty the documentation treats as critical: transaction ids are a finite counter, and old row versions must be frozen before the counter wraps, or the database refuses new writes to protect the data.

blocks.title: How one long transaction bloats a table
items: A reporting transaction opens and takes a snapshot at 09:00 (assumption).
A hot table receives 500 updates per second (assumption); each creates a new row version and leaves the old one.
After one hour the table holds 1.8 million dead versions that vacuum cannot remove, because the report's snapshot might still need them.
At 200 bytes per version (assumption) that is about 360 MB of dead space in the table alone, plus an entry per version in every index.
Every scan of the table now reads the dead versions too, and index-only scans fall back to heap visits because the pages are no longer all-visible.
The report commits; the next vacuum removes the versions but the table file does not shrink, so the space is reused rather than returned.

blocks.text: The design consequences follow. Keep transactions short, especially read-only ones that hold a snapshot, and give long analytical reads a replica. Watch the oldest transaction age and the dead-tuple counts as operational signals. And when a table is updated far more often than it is read, remember that every update is a new version plus an index entry per index: under MVCC the B-tree's update in place is an insert and a mark, with a cleanup debt.

A long-running transaction is a vacuum stop. One idle session that opened a transaction hours ago pins every version written since, in every table, until it commits or is killed. Find them by the age of the oldest open transaction and end them.

The plan is the only honest account of what the engine does with a query, and EXPLAIN prints it. The planner devises a tree of nodes: scans at the leaves, such as a sequential scan, an index scan, a bitmap scan that collects matching row locations from an index first, or an index-only scan; and joins, sorts and aggregates above them. Each node carries an estimated start-up cost, total cost, row count and row width. The costs are in arbitrary units set by the planner's cost parameters, with a sequential page fetch as the traditional unit, so they compare plans against each other, not against a clock.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and adds the actual time, the actual row count and the loop count to each node, and the BUFFERS option adds the pages hit in cache and read from disk. The gap between estimated and actual rows is the first thing to read: a node that expected a hundred rows and saw a million explains the bad join strategy above it, and usually points at stale statistics or a predicate the planner cannot estimate. Read the plan from the innermost node outwards, following the data as it flows up.

blocks.title: Reading a plan, in order
items: Find the node with the largest actual time that is not just the sum of its children; that is where the time goes.
Compare its estimated rows with its actual rows. A factor of 10 or more means the planner was working from wrong information.
Check the scan type at the leaves: a sequential scan on a large table with a selective predicate wants an index; an index scan returning most of the table wants to be a sequential scan.
Look at the buffers: pages read from disk, rather than hit in cache, are the physical I/O the query paid.
Check whether a sort or a hash spilled to disk, which shows as a disk sort method or batches above one.
Only then change something: an index, a rewritten predicate, fresher statistics. Re-run and compare the two plans side by side.

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, o.total
FROM orders o
WHERE o.customer_id = 4821
  AND o.created_at >= now() - interval '30 days'
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- a multicolumn index that matches the predicate and the order:
-- equality on the leading column, a range on the next, and the sort for free
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_created_idx
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);
blocks.caption: The plan before and after the index is the evidence that justifies it. The index is built concurrently so the table keeps taking writes.

blocks.text: Never add an index without the plan that needed it, and never trust an estimate that EXPLAIN ANALYZE has not confirmed on production-sized data. The planner's costs are relative units; the actual times and buffer counts are the measurement.

worked_example.title: Worked example: an event log at 50,000 inserts per second, B-tree against LSM

blocks.text: A product records user events: 50,000 inserts per second of about 200 bytes each, keyed by a random event id, read mostly as recent per-user ranges. The team must choose between a B-tree engine and an LSM engine on a host with one SSD. Every input is an assumption chosen to make the arithmetic concrete; the amplification definitions are the RocksDB tuning guide's.

blocks.title: From the insert rate to disk bandwidth and memory
items: Logical write rate: 50,000 events per second times 200 bytes is 10 MB/s (assumption).
Disk budget: one SSD sustaining about 500 MB/s of writes (assumption from the device sheet).

B-tree, random keys: each insert dirties at least one page of 8 kB somewhere in the tree, and in the worst case each dirty page is written back once per insert, a write amplification of about 40 (8,192 divided by 200).
B-tree disk writes in that worst case: 10 MB/s times 40 is 400 MB/s, four fifths of the disk, before the write-ahead log and the indexes on other columns.

LSM, leveled compaction: a fanout of 10 and about 4 levels on disk give a worst-case write amplification near 40 as well, but the RocksDB wiki notes the per-level factor is usually well under the fanout, so take 20 as the planning value.
LSM disk writes: 10 MB/s times 20 is 200 MB/s, two fifths of the disk, all of it sequential.

Tiered compaction instead: a byte is rewritten about once per size doubling, so a write amplification near 5 gives 50 MB/s, at the price of more files per read and up to double the space during a merge of the largest run.

Read side: with 2 billion events stored (assumption: about 5 days of retention), Bloom filters at 10 bits per key cost 2.5 GB of memory and let a point lookup skip almost every file, a false-positive rate of about one percent.
Space: leveled keeps space amplification near 1.1, so 2 billion events times 200 bytes is 400 GB of data and about 440 GB on disk before compression; tiered needs headroom for the transient doubling.

The decider: write bandwidth. The B-tree spends most of the disk on page rewrites for a workload that reads recent ranges; a leveled LSM halves the disk writes and keeps reads cheap with 2.5 GB of filters, and tiered compaction is the fallback if ingest grows another fivefold.

blocks.caption: The estimate as a reviewer should receive it: one row per quantity, with its formula or source.
rows: 10 MB/s times a write amplification of 40 (8 kB page per 200-byte row)
10 MB/s times a planning write amplification of 20 (fanout 10, under the worst case)
400 GB times a space amplification near 1.1

blocks.text: The B-tree figure is a worst case: a real engine writes a dirty page once per checkpoint interval, not once per row, so the amplification falls as the hot pages absorb several inserts between writes. It falls furthest when keys are sequential, which is why the first question to the team is whether the event id can be time-ordered. If it can, the B-tree's hot pages are the rightmost leaves and the comparison changes; if it must be random, the arithmetic above stands.
